docs.title: qdp-jit
docs.text:
qdp-jit is an implementation of the QDP++ data-parallel API for lattice QCD. Programs written for QDP++, such as Chroma, build against qdp-jit. The difference is in how expressions are evaluated: qdp-jit generates a kernel for each expression at run time with LLVM and runs it on a GPU.

  • GPU backends: CUDA, ROCm and Intel Level Zero. The backend is chosen when qdp-jit is configured (QDP_ENABLE_BACKEND=CUDA|ROCM|L0).
  • Host JIT: when built with QDP_ENABLE_HOST_COMPILER=ON, expressions on scalar (OScalar) values can also be JIT-compiled for the host CPU.

These pages assume you know QDP++. They describe what qdp-jit adds to QDP++ and to earlier qdp-jit versions, and point out where it behaves differently. To build qdp-jit and Chroma, see Download and build. Then start with Concepts, which defines the terms the other pages use.

docs.title: Several lattices in one program
docs.text: QDP++ has one lattice, fixed at QDP_initialize. qdp-jit can hold any number of lattice layouts at the same time, typically a fine lattice and the coarse lattices of a multigrid hierarchy. Coarse layouts are made by blocking an existing one, and a stack of current layouts decides where new fields live. See Layouts and Scopes.

docs.title: Spin and color extents at run time
docs.text: In QDP++ the number of spin components Ns and of colors Nc are compile-time constants. In qdp-jit they are run-time values, carried by each field as its shape. A coarse-grid field with, say, 2 spin components and 24 "colors" uses the same types (LatticeFermion, LatticeColorMatrix, …) as a fine-grid field.

docs.title: Data format and half-precision storage
docs.text: Each field carries a data format: the order of its data in memory and how its floating-point numbers are stored. Floating-point fields can be stored in 16-bit half precision and still be used in ordinary expressions, together with fields stored at full precision.

docs.title: Clear rules for metadata
docs.text: A field's layout, shape and data format are set when it is constructed. Construction and copying says, for each constructor and for assignment, where they come from.

docs.title: Block sums
docs.text: blockSum(expr, blocking) sums an expression over each block of sites of a fine lattice and returns a field on the coarse lattice, one site per block. This is the restriction step of a multigrid solver. See blockSum.

docs.title: Mixed-layout expressions
docs.text: Fields on different layouts can appear in the same expression, for example fine = fine * coarse. Each coarse site's value is used for all fine sites in its block. This is the prolongation step of a multigrid solver. See Mixed-layout expressions.

docs.title: Timing
docs.text: Kernel launches are asynchronous, so a host-side timer measures only the launch. Timing shows how to get correct times with StopWatch. All command-line options are listed in Command-line options.

docs.title: blockSum
docs.text:
blockSum(expr, blocking) divides the lattice into blocks of sites and sums an expression over each block. The result is a field on the coarse layout, with one site per block. In a multigrid solver this is the restriction step: the projection of a fine vector onto the coarse grid.

multi1d<int> blocking(Nd);
blocking = 4;                                   // 4^4 sites per block

LatticeComplexD a = blockSum(localInnerProduct(v, psi), blocking);

docs.title: What it computes
docs.text:
The blocking gives the block size in each dimension. The coarse site y collects the fine sites x with x[mu] / blocking[mu] == y[mu] in every dimension mu, that is the sites from y[mu] * blocking[mu] to (y[mu] + 1) * blocking[mu] - 1. Its value is the sum of the expression over those sites:

multi1d<int> blocking(Nd);
blocking = 2;

LatticeReal delta = zero;
pokeSite(delta, Real(1.0), x);         // x = (3, 1, 0, 2)
LatticeRealD b = blockSum(delta, blocking);
// b is 1 at the coarse site (1, 0, 0, 1) and 0 elsewhere

LatticeRealD n = blockSum(LatticeReal(1.0), blocking);
// n is 16, the number of sites in a block, at every coarse site

Every fine site belongs to exactly one block, so the total is unchanged: sum(blockSum(f, blocking)) equals sum(f).

The sum runs over all sites; there is no version that takes a subset.

docs.title: The result
The blocking
docs.text:
blocking has one entry per dimension (Nd entries) and must divide the lattice size of the expression's layout in every dimension. Otherwise the program aborts:

LatticeLayout::coarsen: blocking 3 1 1 1 does not divide the lattice 4 4 4 4

The coarse layout must fit the node grid, like every layout (see Layouts). Because of this, each block lies entirely on one rank, and blockSum needs no communication between ranks.

docs.title: Expressions as the argument
docs.text:
The argument can be any lattice expression. It is evaluated site by site inside the summing kernel, without a temporary field for the expression:

LatticeComplexD a = blockSum(localInnerProduct(v, psi), blocking);
LatticeRealD    n = blockSum(localNorm2(v), blocking);
LatticeColorMatrixD m = blockSum(u * adj(w), blocking);

An expression that contains a shift is first evaluated into a temporary field on the expression's layout, and the temporary is summed. The result is the same, but it costs the memory and the time of one extra fine field.

docs.title: Repeated blocking
docs.text:
The argument can be on a coarse layout too, so blockings can be applied one after the other. Two blockings in a row give the same field, on the same layout, as one blocking by their product:

auto r1 = blockSum(blockSum(z, b1), b2);
auto r2 = blockSum(z, b1 * b2);        // per dimension
// r1.layout() == r2.layout(), and r1 equals r2

docs.title: blockSum and broadcasting
docs.text:
Assigning a coarse field to a fine one copies each coarse value to every fine site of its block (see Mixed layouts). blockSum is the adjoint of that operation: for a coarse field c and a fine field f,

LatticeComplex pc = c;                 // pc is fine: c broadcast to its blocks
innerProduct(c, blockSum(f, blocking)) == innerProduct(pc, f);   // up to rounding

So the restriction blockSum(localInnerProduct(v, psi), blocking) and the prolongation psi += v * c with a coarse c form an adjoint pair, as a multigrid solver needs. Scopes shows a complete restriction onto a coarse vector with several components.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
blockSum runs one kernel, generated for the expression, the shapes and the data formats of its leaves, and cached like other kernels.

Each coarse site is handled by a group of threads. Each thread in the group reads a share of the block's fine sites, evaluates the expression there and adds up the values. The group then combines its partial sums in shared memory and one thread writes the result to the coarse site. With a group size of 1, one thread sums the whole block and no shared memory is used.

The group size is a power of 2, at most 32 and no larger than the block size rounded up to a power of 2. qdp-jit chooses the smallest group size that gives enough threads to fill the GPU: large blocks on a small coarse lattice get large groups, small blocks on a large coarse lattice get one thread each. The command-line option

-blocksum N

sets the group size to N for every blockSum; N must be a power of 2, otherwise the program aborts with blockSum: -blocksum N is not a power of 2. The result does not depend on the group size apart from rounding. Use the option only to compare timings.

docs.text: Function Description blockSum(const QDPType<T,C>& f, const multi1d<int>& blocking) the block sums of a field blockSum(const QDPExpr<RHS,OLattice<T>>& expr, const multi1d<int>& blocking) the block sums of an expression LatticeLayout::coarsen(const multi1d<int>& blocking) the layout of the result, see Layouts -blocksum N command-line option: N threads per coarse site, a power of 2; 0 (the default) chooses automatically int qdp_jit_config_get_blocksum(), void qdp_jit_config_set_blocksum(int n) the same setting in code

docs.title: Download and build
docs.text: The easiest way to build qdp-jit together with Chroma is the build package at github.com/fwinter/package. Its scripts download the sources of LLVM, QMP, qdp-jit and Chroma, and build and install them in order, for one GPU architecture.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Before you start, make sure the following are available, on a cluster usually by loading the corresponding modules:

  • the GPU software stack: the CUDA toolkit (NVIDIA), ROCm (AMD) or oneAPI with Level Zero (Intel);
  • an MPI installation with its compiler wrappers (mpicxx, mpicc);
  • a C++ compiler, CMake, git and wget.

Get the package:

git clone https://github.com/fwinter/package.git
cd package

docs.title: 1. Choose the GPU architecture
docs.text:
Each architecture has its own download script and its own directory of build scripts:

GPU Download script Directory NVIDIA download_sources_cuda.sh cuda/ AMD download_sources_rocm.sh rocm-jit-noquda/ Intel download_sources_intel.sh level-zero/

The examples below are for NVIDIA GPUs; replace cuda by the script and directory of your architecture.

docs.title: 2. Download the sources
docs.text:
From the root of the package, run the download script:

./download_sources_cuda.sh

It clones QMP, qdp-jit and Chroma and downloads the LLVM sources, all into src/. Unpacking LLVM takes a moment.

docs.title: 3. Configure the environment
docs.text:
Change to the directory of your architecture and edit env.sh:

cd cuda

env.sh is read by every build script. Set the compilers to your MPI compiler wrappers:

export CXX=mpicxx
export CC=mpicc

and add anything else your system needs, such as module load lines or paths. On some systems the wrappers have other names; on Cray systems, for example, they are CC and cc.

The directory also holds env_*.sh files for particular machines (for example env_perlmutter.sh in cuda/, env_frontier.sh in rocm-jit-noquda/). Use one of them as a starting point if your machine is among them.

The rest of env.sh sets where the build happens. Keep it unless you want another location:

Variable Default Contents SRCROOT ../src the sources downloaded in step 2 BUILDROOT ./build one build directory per package INSTALLROOT ./install one install directory per package

docs.title: 4. Build
docs.text:
./build_all.sh

build_all.sh runs the build scripts in order: LLVM, QMP, qdp-jit (build_qdpxx.sh) and Chroma (build_chroma.sh). Building LLVM takes the longest. When it has finished, install/ holds:

Directory Contents install/llvm-* LLVM install/qmp QMP install/qdpxx qdp-jit install/chroma Chroma, with the executable install/chroma/bin/chroma

docs.title: Rebuilding a part
docs.text:
Each package has its own build script, which can be run on its own, from the architecture directory. A script removes its build directory first, so each run is a clean build.

After a change to qdp-jit, rebuild qdp-jit and then Chroma, which is compiled against qdp-jit's headers:

./build_qdpxx.sh
./build_chroma.sh

clean.sh removes the build and install directories of QMP, qdp-jit and Chroma (LLVM is kept).

docs.title: Build options of qdp-jit
docs.text:
build_qdpxx.sh configures qdp-jit with CMake. To change an option, edit the cmake command in that script. The most important options:

Option Values Description QDP_ENABLE_BACKEND CUDA, ROCM, L0 the GPU backend QDP_PRECISION single, double (default) the precision of Real, LatticeFermion, … QDP_LAYOUT cb2 (default), lexico, cb3d the site layout, see Layouts QDP_ND, QDP_NC, QDP_NS 4, 3, 4 (default) the number of dimensions, and the initial current shape (Ns, Nc), see Shape QDP_ENABLE_HOST_COMPILER ON, OFF (default) also JIT-compile scalar expressions for the CPU LLVM_DIR a path the LLVM installation to use; qdp-jit needs LLVM 22 or newer. With the ROCm backend it defaults to the LLVM that comes with ROCm

docs.title: Using qdp-jit in your own program
docs.text:
qdp-jit installs a CMake package configuration. A CMake project needs C and C++ enabled (QMP looks for MPI's C interface); linking QDPXX::qdp compiles it as C++20:

project(my_program C CXX)

find_package(QDPXX REQUIRED)
target_link_libraries(my_program QDPXX::qdp)

Configure it with the locations of qdp-jit, QMP and LLVM, as build_chroma.sh does for Chroma:

cmake <source> \
-DQDPXX_DIR=<package>/cuda/install/qdpxx/lib/cmake/QDPXX \
-DQMP_DIR=<package>/cuda/install/qmp/lib/cmake/QMP \
-DLLVM_DIR=<package>/cuda/install/llvm-<version>/lib/cmake/llvm

To run on several GPUs, start one MPI rank per GPU and give the grid of ranks with -geom; see Command-line options.

docs.title: Concepts
docs.text: This page defines the terms used on the other pages. Each term is defined once here; the pages that follow go into detail.

docs.title: Lattice size
docs.text:
The global extent of a lattice in each of the Nd dimensions, for example 8 8 8 16. As in QDP++, the lattice size of the first lattice is set with Layout::setLattSize(nrow) before Layout::create().

const multi1d<int>& nrow = Layout::lattSize();   // of the current layout
size_t volume            = Layout::vol();        // product of nrow

In qdp-jit there can be several lattices, each with its own lattice size. The functions in the Layout namespace (Layout::lattSize(), Layout::vol(), Layout::sitesOnNode(), …) return the values of the current layout. The same functions are members of a LatticeLayout object, for example layout.lattSize().

docs.title: Machine geometry
docs.text:
The logical grid of MPI ranks (nodes), one extent per dimension, returned by Layout::logicalSize(). Set it on the command line with

-geom X Y Z T

Without -geom, QMP chooses the geometry. The geometry is fixed when the first layout is created and is the same for every layout created later.

docs.title: Subgrid
docs.text:
The part of a lattice that lives on one rank: the lattice size divided by the machine geometry in each dimension.

const multi1d<int>& sub = Layout::subgridLattSize();  // lattice size / geometry
int sites               = Layout::sitesOnNode();      // product of sub

Every lattice size must therefore be divisible by the machine geometry in every dimension. This holds for coarse lattices too, which limits how far a lattice can be coarsened on a given number of ranks. See Layouts.

docs.title: Layout
docs.text: A LatticeLayout is a lattice size together with its site tables: which rank holds a site, the site's linear index on that rank, and the reverse map from rank and index to coordinates. The first layout is created as in QDP++, with Layout::setLattSize(nrow) and Layout::create() after QDP_initialize. Further layouts, typically coarser ones, are created from it. A LatticeLayout is a small handle; two handles are equal when they refer to the same layout. See Layouts.

docs.title: Current layout
docs.text: qdp-jit keeps a stack of layouts. Its top, Layout::current(), is the layout that default-constructed fields are created on and that the Layout:: functions refer to. At start-up the stack holds the first layout. See Layouts and Scopes.

docs.title: Shape
docs.text: A field's Shape is its pair of extents (Ns, Nc): the number of spin and color components. In QDP++ these are compile-time constants; in qdp-jit they are run-time values, so fields of the same C++ type can have different shapes. A field's shape is f.shape(). Like layouts, shapes have a stack, and its top, Shape::current(), is used for new fields. At start-up it holds the Ns and Nc that qdp-jit was configured with. See Shape.

docs.title: Data format
docs.text: A field's JitDataFormat describes how its data is stored in memory: the order of the site and component indices (JitDataOrder), and whether floating-point numbers are stored at their native precision or as 16-bit halves (JitStorage). A field's data format is f.data_format(). See Data format.

docs.title: Field
docs.text:
A lattice field (OLattice, for example LatticeFermion) or a scalar (OScalar, for example Real or Complex). Besides its data, every lattice field carries three pieces of metadata:

Metadata Accessor layout f.layout() shape f.shape() data format f.data_format()

Where these come from when a field is constructed, copied or assigned is described in Construction and copying.

docs.title: Expression and leaf
docs.text: An expression is a QDP++ expression such as u * shift(psi, FORWARD, mu) + chi. qdp-jit compiles each expression into a kernel the first time it is evaluated and reuses the kernel when the same expression is evaluated again. The leaves of an expression are its operands: the fields and scalars it reads (u, psi and chi above). In qdp-jit the leaves of one expression can have different layouts, shapes and data formats; the rules are on the pages for shapes, data formats and mixed layouts.

docs.title: Construction and copying
docs.text:
Every lattice field carries a layout, a shape and a data format. All three are set when the field is constructed and never change afterwards. This page says where each constructor takes them from, and what assignment does with them.

There are three sources:

  • the ambient settings: the current layout Layout::current(), the current shape Shape::current() and the default data format, all set by scopes;
  • a source field the new field is copied from;
  • an expression the new field is computed from.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
Construction Layout Shape Data format T f; T f = zero; T f = 1.5; current current default T f(shape) T f(shape, zero) current shape default T f(layout, shape) layout shape default T f(format) current current format T f(a) T f = a (copy) a's a's a's T f(a) with a of another type, e.g. LatticeFermionD f(aF) a's a's a's T f(shape, a) a's shape a's T f(expr) T f = expr the finest leaf's the expression's default T f(expr) with only scalar leaves, T f(s) with s a scalar current the expression's default T f(std::move(a)), a field returned by value a's a's a's

"Current" and "default" mean the values in effect where the constructor runs. In every row, extents the type does not have are dropped (a LatticeColorMatrix has Ns = 1), and an index the source or the expression does not have takes its extent from the current shape (a LatticeColorMatrix made from a LatticeReal expression gets the current Nc). See Shape.

docs.title: Default construction
docs.text:
A field constructed without a source takes everything from the ambient settings:

{
LayoutShapeScope coarse_grid(coarse, 2, 24);
JitDataFormatScope half(JitDataFormat(JitDataOrder::SiteFast, JitStorage::Half));
LatticeFermion psi;          // coarse, (2, 24), half
LatticeFermion chi = zero;   // the same, set to zero
}

Constructors with a Shape, a LatticeLayout and Shape, or a JitDataFormat argument override the corresponding ambient setting and take the others from the ambient settings. See Layouts, Shape and Data format.

docs.title: Copies
docs.text:
A copy takes all three from its source, whatever the ambient settings are:

LatticeFermion psi_c = make_coarse_half_fermion();  // coarse, (2, 24), half

LatticeFermion  a(psi_c);     // coarse, (2, 24), half
LatticeFermion  b = psi_c;    // the same
LatticeFermionD d(psi_c);     // the same, at double precision

This also holds for a conversion to another precision (LatticeFermionD from a LatticeFermionF), except that an integer or boolean field is always stored natively.

T f(shape, a) takes the layout and the format from a and the shape from the argument. shape must have the same extents as a (after dropping the extents T does not have); otherwise the program aborts with OLattice: Incompatible tensor dimensions: … (OScalar: … for a scalar).

A named type that fixes an extent, made from a plain field, keeps the source's other extent and requires the fixed one to match:

LatticeFermion f(Shape(4, 5));
LatticeDiracFermion d(f);        // (4, 5), whatever the current Nc
LatticeFermion h(Shape(2, 5));
LatticeDiracFermion e(h);        // aborts: Ns = 4 is required

docs.title: Fields computed from an expression
docs.text:
A field constructed from an expression is computed on the finest layout among the expression's leaves (the one with the largest volume). Its shape is the shape of the expression, and its data format is the default, whatever the formats of the leaves:

LatticeFermion e1 = psi_c + psi_c;               // coarse, (2, 24), default format
LatticeFermion e2(shift(psi_c, FORWARD, 0));     // the same
LatticeComplex e3 = c_coarse * localInnerProduct(psi, psi);   // fine: psi is finer

The ambient layout plays no part as long as the expression has a lattice leaf. An expression of scalars only, such as LatticeReal r = Real(1) + Real(2), and a field made from a scalar, LatticeFermion f(s), are on the current layout.

Mixing layouts in one expression is described in Mixed layouts.

docs.title: Moves and return values
docs.text:
A move takes over the source's storage together with its layout, shape and format. Returning a field by value is therefore cheap and keeps the field's metadata, even when the function opened scopes:

LatticeFermion make_coarse_half_fermion()
{
LayoutShapeScope coarse_grid(coarse, 2, 24);
JitDataFormatScope half(JitDataFormat(JitDataOrder::SiteFast, JitStorage::Half));
LatticeFermion c;
gaussian(c);
return c;                    // the caller gets a coarse, (2, 24), half field
}

docs.title: Assignment
docs.text:
Assignment never changes the destination's layout, shape or data format. It converts the right-hand side to them:

Rule Shape The right-hand side must have the destination's extents, except for an index its type does not have. Otherwise the program aborts with OLattice: Incompatible tensor dimensions: …. See Shape. Data format The values are converted to the destination's format: assigning to a half-precision field rounds them. See Data format. Layout The right-hand side may live on a coarser layout whose blocks fit the destination's: each coarse value is broadcast to its block of fine sites. A right-hand side on a finer or incompatible layout aborts with mixed-layout expression: the destination lattice … is not a multiple of the operand lattice …. See Mixed layouts. 
LatticeFermion h(JitDataFormat(JitDataOrder::SiteFast, JitStorage::Half));
h = psi;                       // still half: psi's values, rounded

LatticeFermion f(fine, Shape(2, 24));
f = psi_c;                     // still fine: psi_c broadcast to the fine sites

To get a field with the right-hand side's metadata, construct a new one instead of assigning to an existing one.

docs.title: Move assignment
docs.text: a = std::move(b) takes over b's storage if a and b have the same layout, shape and data format and b owns its storage. b then holds a's old storage and remains a valid field that can be assigned to. In all other cases move assignment is a copy assignment, following the rules above, and b is unchanged.

docs.title: Arrays of fields
docs.text:
A multi1d of fields constructs its elements by default construction, so they take the ambient settings at the point where the array is sized:

multi1d<LatticeColorMatrix> u_h;
{
JitDataFormatScope half(JitDataFormat(JitDataOrder::SiteFast, JitStorage::Half));
u_h.resize(Nd);              // Nd half-precision fields
}

Copying an array copies each element with its metadata: multi1d<LatticeFermion> b(a), and c = a with c empty, give elements with the layouts, shapes and formats of a's elements. Assigning to an array that already has the same size, d = a, assigns element by element and keeps d's metadata.

docs.title: Scalars
docs.text:
Scalars (OScalar, for example Complex or ColorMatrix) have a shape but no layout or data format.

Construction Shape T s; T s = zero; current T s(shape) shape T s(t), T s(expr) t's or the expression's; an index the source lacks gets the current extent

Unlike a lattice field, a scalar takes the right-hand side's shape on assignment when it does not fit, so s = sum(psi) works for a psi of any shape. See Shape.

docs.title: Data format
docs.text:
Every lattice field has a data format, f.data_format(), which says how the field's data is laid out in device memory and how floating-point numbers are stored there. A data format has two parts:

struct JitDataFormat
{
JitDataOrder order   = JitDataOrder::SiteFast;   // or SiteSlow
JitStorage   storage = JitStorage::Native;       // or Half
};

The data format is a property of the field's data, not of its type: a LatticeFermion stored in half precision is still a LatticeFermion and is used in expressions like any other. Scalars (OScalar) have no data format.

docs.title: Order
docs.text:
JitDataOrder gives the order of the site index relative to the spin, color and complex indices on the device:

Order Device layout SiteFast (default) the site index runs fastest: for each component, the values of all sites are contiguous ("structure of arrays") SiteSlow the site index runs slowest: all components of a site are contiguous ("array of structures")

SiteFast gives coalesced memory access on GPUs and is the default.

docs.title: Storage
docs.text:
JitStorage says how floating-point numbers are stored on the device:

Storage Device storage Native (default) at the precision of the field's type: float for LatticeFermionF, double for LatticeFermionD Half as 16-bit IEEE half-precision numbers

A half-precision field takes half the device memory of a single-precision field and a quarter of a double-precision one, and moving it costs correspondingly less memory bandwidth. Kernels read the stored half values, convert them to the precision of the field's type, and compute at that precision. When a kernel writes to a half-precision field, it rounds the result to the nearest half value (ties to even).

Half precision has an 11-bit significand, about 3 decimal digits, and a limited range:

Value stored Read back 1.0/3.0 0.333251953125 1000.3 1000.5 65504 (largest half value) 65504 70000 inf 1e-6 1.0132789611816406e-06 (subnormal) 1e-8 0

Values above 65504 become infinite. Scale data such as gauge links or normalized vectors so that it stays within range; isfinite(f) tells whether a field holds only finite values.

Integer and boolean fields (LatticeInteger, LatticeBoolean, …) are always stored natively, see below.

docs.title: The default data format
docs.text:
New fields get the default data format unless the constructor takes the format from somewhere else (see Construction and copying). At start-up the default is SiteFast and Native.

The command-line option

-default-data-order-site-slow

changes the default order to SiteSlow. There is no command-line option for half storage; use a scope or a constructor argument.

Within a block, set the default with a JitDataFormatScope:

JitDataFormat half(JitDataOrder::SiteFast, JitStorage::Half);
{
JitDataFormatScope scope(half);
multi1d<LatticeColorMatrix> u_half(Nd);   // all stored in half precision
}

The current default is qdp_jit_config_get_default_data_format().

docs.title: Creating a field with a given format
docs.text:
Pass the format to the constructor:

LatticeFermion psi_h(JitDataFormat(JitDataOrder::SiteFast, JitStorage::Half));

This ignores the default. Note that JitDataFormat(order) alone means native storage, and JitDataFormat() means SiteFast, Native whatever the default is.

docs.title: Where a field's format comes from
docs.text:
Construction Data format T f;, T f = zero;, T f(shape); the default T f(format) format T f(g), T f = g (copy) g's format LatticeFermionD f(g) with g a LatticeFermionF g's format T f(expr), T f = expr (expression) the default, whatever the formats of the leaves

Assignment never changes the destination's format: f = g converts g's values to f's format. Assigning a half-precision field to a native one gives the rounded values at native precision; assigning a native field to a half-precision one rounds them.

For multi1d of fields, copying keeps each element's format: multi1d<LatticeFermion> b(a) and assignment to an empty array c = a give elements with the formats of a's elements. Assigning to an array that already has elements, d = a with d of size 3, assigns element by element and keeps d's formats.

The full rules, together with those for the layout and the shape, are in Construction and copying.

docs.title: Mixing formats in an expression
docs.text:
The leaves of an expression can have different data formats. Each leaf is read in its own format and the result is written in the destination's format:

LatticeColorMatrix u_h(JitDataFormat(JitDataOrder::SiteSlow, JitStorage::Half));
LatticeFermion     psi_h(JitDataFormat(JitDataOrder::SiteFast, JitStorage::Half));
u_h   = u;
psi_h = psi;

LatticeFermion chi = u_h * psi_h + shift(psi_h, FORWARD, 0);   // native result

The result is exactly what the same expression gives with native fields that hold the rounded values of u_h and psi_h. The same holds for shifts in both directions, for subsets (chi[rb[0]] += …), for coarse-grid fields and for reductions: norm2, innerProduct and globalMax of a half-precision field equal those of a native field holding the same rounded values.

Host access works as for native fields: peekSite returns, and pokeSite stores, values at the precision of the field's type, rounded to half on the way in.

docs.title: Integer and boolean fields
docs.text:

docs.title: Layouts
docs.text: QDP++ has a single lattice. qdp-jit can hold several lattice layouts at once, typically the fine lattice and the coarse lattices of a multigrid hierarchy. This page covers what a layout is, how coarse layouts are made, the layout stack, and which parts of QDP++ follow the current layout.

docs.title: What a layout is
docs.text:
A LatticeLayout is a lattice size together with its site tables: for every site, which rank holds it and its linear index on that rank, and the reverse map from rank and index back to coordinates (see Concepts).

The first layout is set up exactly as in QDP++:

QDP_initialize(&argc, &argv);

multi1d<int> nrow(Nd);
nrow = 16;
nrow[3] = 32;
Layout::setLattSize(nrow);
Layout::create();          // creates the first (fine) layout

LatticeLayout fine = Layout::current();

A LatticeLayout is a small value-type handle; copy it freely. Two handles compare equal when they refer to the same layout, and since there is only one layout per lattice size (see below), that is the same as having the same lattice size. Handles have < and std::hash, so they can be keys of std::map and std::unordered_map. A default-constructed LatticeLayout() refers to no layout; its index() is -1.

Layouts are never destroyed before QDP_finalize. A handle stays valid for the whole program from its point of creation.

docs.title: Creating coarse layouts
docs.text:
There are two ways to get another layout. Both return the layout without changing the current layout.

By blocking an existing layout. layout.coarsen(blocking) divides the lattice size by blocking in each dimension:

multi1d<int> blocking(Nd);
blocking = 2;                                       // 2^4 blocks
LatticeLayout coarse = fine.coarsen(blocking);      // 8 8 8 16

The blocking must divide the lattice size in every dimension, otherwise the program stops with

LatticeLayout::coarsen: blocking 3 1 1 1 does not divide the lattice 4 4 4 4

A blocking of 1 in every dimension returns the layout itself.

By lattice size. Layout::find_or_create(nrow) returns the layout with lattice size nrow, creating it if there is none yet:

multi1d<int> nrow(Nd);
nrow = 4;
LatticeLayout l = Layout::find_or_create(nrow);

coarsen is a shorthand for find_or_create(lattSize() / blocking). There is never more than one layout for a given lattice size, so asking for the same size again, by either function, returns the same layout.

docs.title: Repeated blocking
docs.text:
Because layouts are identified by their lattice size, blocking in steps gives the same layout as blocking in one go:

multi1d<int> bt(Nd), bs(Nd), b(Nd);
bt = 1; bt[3] = 2;               // 1 1 1 2
bs = 2; bs[3] = 1;               // 2 2 2 1
b  = 2;                          // 2 2 2 2

assert(fine.coarsen(bt).coarsen(bs) == fine.coarsen(b));

A multigrid hierarchy can therefore be built level by level, each level by coarsening the one above it, and fields on a level can be compared or combined with fields made from a different chain of blockings, as long as the lattice sizes agree.

docs.title: Each layout must fit the node grid
docs.text:
All layouts share the machine geometry: the logical grid of ranks, set with -geom or chosen by QMP when the first layout is created (see Concepts). Every rank holds part of every layout. A lattice size therefore fits only if, in every dimension:

  • it is divisible by the number of ranks in that dimension, and
  • the resulting subgrid extent is a multiple of the minimal extent of the site layout qdp-jit was built with (QDP_LAYOUT):
QDP_LAYOUT minimal subgrid extent lexico 1 in every dimension cb2 (default) 2 in x, 1 otherwise cb3d 2 in x, 1 otherwise

This applies to coarse layouts too, and limits how far a lattice can be coarsened on a given number of ranks. If a layout does not fit, creating it stops the program, whether through coarsen or find_or_create:

LayoutData::create - problem size 4 4 4 1 does not fit the node grid 1 1 1 2
with a subgrid that is a multiple of 2 1 1 1

This is with the lattice 4 4 4 4 on 2 ranks (-geom 1 1 1 2), blocked by 4 in time: the coarse lattice has 1 site in time, which cannot be split over 2 ranks. With -geom 2 1 1 1 and the cb2 site layout, blocking by 2 in x fails too: each rank would get 1 site in x, and cb2 needs an even number.

Two earlier checks report the same problem with other messages: a lattice whose volume is not divisible by the number of ranks stops with LayoutData::create - problem size not divisible by number of processors, and one whose size is not a multiple of the minimal subgrid extent (for example a coarse lattice with 1 site in x on one rank with cb2) stops with LayoutData::create - Error: problem size not multiple of smallest size allowed for this type of layout.

Layout::fits_node_grid(nrow) returns whether a lattice size fits, without creating a layout. Use it to choose a blocking that works on the current number of ranks.

multi1d<int> nrow = fine.lattSize() / blocking;
if (!Layout::fits_node_grid(nrow))
QDPIO::cerr << "blocking too coarse for this node grid\n";

docs.title: The layout stack
docs.text:
qdp-jit keeps a stack of layouts. The layout on top is the current layout, Layout::current(). After Layout::create() the stack holds the first layout.

Layout::push(coarse);        // coarse is now current
LatticeFermion c;            // a field on the coarse layout
Layout::pop();               // fine is current again

push and pop must be balanced. Layout::push(LatticeLayout()) stops the program (Layout::push called with invalid layout -1), and so does a call of Layout::current() once the stack has been popped empty. Rather than calling push and pop by hand, use a LayoutScope, which pops when it goes out of scope, also when an exception is thrown.

Layouts can be pushed in any order and any number of times. Pushing a layout that is already on the stack is allowed.

docs.title: A field keeps its layout
docs.text:
A field's layout is fixed when the field is constructed (see Construction and copying for where it comes from). Popping the stack does not change the layout of fields created while the layout was current:

{
LayoutScope scope(coarse);
LatticeReal t = zero;      // on the coarse layout
...
}                            // fine is current again; t is gone

LayoutScope scope(coarse);
LatticeReal d = zero;        // on the coarse layout
scope.close();               // pop now, d stays alive

assert(d.layout() == coarse);
d[rb[0]] = Real(1.0);        // still evaluated on the coarse layout
Double s = sum(d);           // coarse volume / 2

docs.title: Creating a field on a given layout
docs.text:
A field can also be created on a layout without touching the stack. The constructor OLattice(LatticeLayout, Shape) makes a field on the layout and with the shape you pass, whichever layout and shape are current:

LayoutShapeScope coarse_grid(coarse, 2, 24);   // coarse layout, Ns=2, Nc=24

LatticeFermion c;                               // coarse, Ns=2, Nc=24
LatticeFermion f(fine, Shape(Ns, Nc));          // fine, the configured Ns and Nc
LatticeColorMatrix u(fine, Shape(Ns, Nc));      // fine, shape (1, Nc)

There is no constructor that takes only a layout, on purpose: inside a scope like the one above, the current shape belongs to the coarse grid, and a fine field would silently get it. Extents that the type does not have are set to 1: u above has the shape (1, Nc), since a color matrix has no spin index. The data format is the current default, as for a default-constructed field (see Data format).

This is the simplest way to make a field on another layout in the middle of code that runs on the current one, for example a fine-grid temporary inside a coarse-grid scope. The fields are ordinary fields: f = psi; with a fine psi works as usual.

docs.title: Operations use the field's layout
docs.text:
Operations on a field, such as assignment, shift, subsets, random and reductions, use the field's own layout, not the current one. The current layout matters only where no field says which layout to use; the next section lists these places.

Assignment does not move a field to another layout

c = zero; inside a LayoutScope(coarse) does not put c on the coarse layout if c was constructed on the fine one. Assignment keeps the destination's layout. Construct the field while the layout you want is current, or pass the layout to the constructor: LatticeReal c(coarse, Shape());.

docs.title: Lattice coordinates
docs.text:
Layout::latticeCoordinate(mu) returns a LatticeInteger on the current layout, holding each site's coordinate in direction mu. To get coordinates that match a given field, make the field's layout current first:

LatticeFermion mask_boundary(const LatticeFermion& in, const multi1d<int>& block, int mu)
{
LayoutScope scope(in.layout());
LatticeReal one = 1.0, nil = zero;
LatticeReal m = where((Layout::latticeCoordinate(mu) + 1) % block[mu] == 0, one, nil);
return in * m;
}

docs.title: Random numbers
docs.text:
Each layout has its own random number generator state. When a layout is created, its seed is set to the same default value as the first layout's; seeding one layout does not seed the others. To seed a coarse layout, make it current:

RNG::setrn(seed);                      // seeds the fine layout only
{
LayoutScope scope(coarse);
RNG::setrn(coarse_seed);             // seeds the coarse layout
}

random(f) and gaussian(f) for a lattice field draw from the generator of f's layout, whichever layout is current. Drawing on a coarse layout leaves the fine layout's stream unchanged. random(x) for a scalar draws from the current layout's generator.

docs.title: Subsets and maps
docs.text:
The predefined sets and subsets (all, even, odd, rb, rb3, mcb) and the nearest-neighbour shifts (shift(f, FORWARD, mu), …) are set up on every layout when it is created. They work on fields of any layout, with no further action.

A Set or Map you make yourself is different: Set::make(fn) and Map::make(fn) compute their tables for the current layout only, and the function fn sees that layout's coordinates (for example through Layout::lattSize()). To use one on another layout, call make again with that layout current. The tables for the other layouts are kept:

Set blocks;
blocks.make(MyBlockFunc());            // tables for the fine layout
{
LayoutScope scope(coarse);
blocks.make(MyBlockFunc());          // and for the coarse layout
}
// blocks[i] now works on fine and on coarse fields

Using a user-made Set or Map on a layout it was not made for stops the program:

Subset numSiteTable: no site tables for layout 1
Map make_lazy: map not made for layout 1

The site tables of a subset are queried for a given layout with s.siteTable(layout), s.numSiteTable(layout), s.isElement(layout, i) and so on. The versions without a layout argument use the current layout.

docs.title: Mixed-layout expressions
docs.text:
An expression can combine fields on different layouts, as long as each field's lattice divides the lattice the expression is evaluated on. The typical case is a coarse field in a fine expression:

LatticeFermion psi;                 // fine
LatticeComplex c_coarse;            // made on the coarse layout
// ...
psi += v * c_coarse;                // v fine: the prolongation step

Each coarse value is used for every fine site of its block. No temporary fine copy of the coarse field is made: the kernel reads the coarse field directly.

docs.title: Which coarse site a fine site reads
docs.text:
The expression is evaluated on one layout, the expression layout (see below). For a field on another layout, the blocking is the ratio of the lattice sizes, b[mu] = L_expr[mu] / L_field[mu], and the fine site x reads the site y with

y[mu] = x[mu] / b[mu]          (integer division, in every dimension mu)

These are the same blocks that blockSum sums over. With a fine lattice 8 8 8 8 and a coarse field on fine.coarsen(b) with b = 1 2 2 4, the fine site (7, 5, 6, 7) reads the coarse site (7, 2, 3, 1).

The blocking is worked out from the lattice sizes alone, so it does not matter how the coarse layout was made: with coarsen, with repeated coarsen calls, or with Layout::find_or_create (there is only one layout per lattice size, see Layouts). Each block lies on one rank, so reading a coarse field needs no communication.

docs.title: The expression layout
docs.text:
Evaluation Expression layout dest = expr, dest += expr, … the layout of dest T f = expr, T f(expr) the finest leaf of expr, the one with the largest volume sum(expr), norm2(expr), innerProduct(a, b), blockSum(expr, b), … the finest leaf

Assignment never changes the destination's layout (see Construction and copying). A field constructed from an expression gets the finest leaf's layout:

LatticeReal g = f * a2 + a4;        // f fine, a2 and a4 on two coarser layouts:
// g is fine
LatticeReal h = a2 * a4;            // h is on a2's layout
f = a2 * a4;                        // still fine: both broadcast to f

Scalars (Real, Complex, …) can appear in any expression and are the same at every site.

docs.title: Restrictions
docs.text:
Every field in the expression must be on a lattice that divides the expression layout's lattice in every dimension. The fine-to-coarse direction is therefore an error:

coarse = fine;
// mixed-layout expression: the destination lattice 4 4 4 4 is not a multiple
// of the operand lattice 8 8 8 8

To go from fine to coarse, use blockSum.

The same error happens between two coarsenings of which neither divides the other. With a fine lattice 8 8 8 8, ax on fine.coarsen(2 1 1 1) (lattice 4 8 8 8) and ay on fine.coarsen(1 2 1 1) (lattice 8 4 8 8):

Expression Result f = ax + ay with f fine works: both divide 8 8 8 8 ax = ay aborts: 4 8 8 8 is not a multiple of 8 4 8 8 LatticeReal e = ax + ay aborts: both have the same volume, and one of them becomes the expression layout

The shapes and the data formats of the leaves follow the usual rules (see Shape and Data format), independently of their layouts.

docs.title: Subsets
docs.text:
A subset on the left-hand side is a subset of the destination's layout:

f[rb[0]]  = c_coarse;               // the even sites of f get c_coarse
f[rb[1]] += c_coarse * f;

A reduction over a subset, sum(f * c_coarse, rb[1]), also uses the subset of the expression layout.

docs.title: Shifts
docs.text:
A shift moves by one site of the expression layout, so the field inside a shift must be on the expression layout:

f2 = shift(f, FORWARD, mu) * c_coarse;   // works: f is fine
f2 = f * shift(c_coarse, FORWARD, mu);   // aborts

The second line stops with

shift in a mixed-layout expression: the shifted field is on the lattice 4 4 4 4,
the expression is evaluated on the lattice 8 8 8 8. Shift the field on its own
layout first, or assign it to a field on the expression's layout and shift that

There are two different things that line could mean, and each can be written out:

// the neighbouring coarse site: shift on the coarse layout first
LatticeComplex cs(c_coarse.layout(), c_coarse.shape());
cs = shift(c_coarse, FORWARD, mu);
f2 = f * cs;

// the neighbouring fine site: broadcast first, then shift on the fine layout
LatticeComplex cb;                  // fine
cb = c_coarse;
f2 = f * shift(cb, FORWARD, mu);

The two give different results: the first moves by a whole block, the second by one fine site, which crosses into the next block only at the block's edge.

docs.title: Reductions
docs.text:
sum, sumMulti, norm2, innerProduct and the other reductions accept mixed-layout expressions. They run over the sites of the finest leaf's layout, and give the same result as with the coarse fields broadcast to that layout first:

sum(f * c_coarse)                   // a sum over all fine sites
innerProduct(f, c_coarse)           // the same as innerProduct(f, cb), cb = c_coarse
sum(f * c_coarse, rb[1])            // over the odd fine sites

blockSum of a mixed-layout expression blocks the finest leaf's layout, see blockSum.

docs.title: Command-line options
docs.text:
QDP_initialize(&argc, &argv) reads the options below from the command line. They are not removed from argv, so the program sees them too. Options that qdp-jit does not know are ignored, and QMP reads its own options as well.

mpirun -np 4 ./my_program -geom 1 1 2 2 -poolsize 20g -timing-run

At start-up the program prints the resulting settings: the memory pool size, the code generation options and the launch configuration.

An option without its value, for example -blocksize as the last argument, stops the program with QDP_initialize: -blocksize needs 1 value.

Memory sizes are a number with an optional suffix k, m, g or t (powers of 1024): 5000m, 20g, 1.5g. Anything else stops the program with Invalid memory size: … (expected a number with an optional k, m, g or t suffix).

See Concepts -iogeom Px Py Pz Pt the grid of I/O nodes, as in QDP++ -use-gpu N use device N. Without it, each rank uses the device local rank % number of devices, with the local rank taken from the environment variables of the MPI launcher (PMI_RANK, MV2_COMM_WORLD_LOCAL_RANK, OMPI_COMM_WORLD_LOCAL_RANK or SLURM_LOCALID). If none is set, device 0 is used and a warning is printed -V verbose output from QMP -debug-layout print the lattice and configuration summary each time a layout is created; without it, the summary is printed only for the first layout. Also print the site tables built for mixed-layout expressions and blockSum, and their cleanup at the end of the run

docs.title: Scopes
docs.text:
New fields take their layout, shape and data format from the current settings (see Concepts). Scopes change these settings for a block of code and restore them at the end of the block. They are the usual way to work on a coarse grid.

Scope Sets Restores at the end LayoutScope(layout) the current layout the previous layout ShapeScope(shape) the current shape the previous shape LayoutShapeScope(layout, ns, nc) layout and shape both LayoutShapeScope(field) field's layout and shape both JitDataFormatScope(format) the default data format the previous format

All scopes are RAII objects: the constructor sets, the destructor restores, also when the block is left by an exception. They cannot be copied or moved.

A scope changes only what new fields get. Fields that already exist keep their layout, shape and data format, and inside a scope they can be used as before:

LatticeFermion psi;                      // fine, Ns=4, Nc=3
{
LayoutShapeScope coarse_grid(coarse, 2, 24);
LatticeFermion chi = psi;              // a copy: fine, Ns=4, Nc=3, like psi
LatticeFermion c;                      // coarse, Ns=2, Nc=24
}

docs.title: LayoutScope
docs.text:
explicit LayoutScope(LatticeLayout layout);
void close();

Pushes layout onto the layout stack and pops it at the end of the scope. close() pops it early; calling close() again, or the destructor after close(), does nothing.

LayoutScope changes only the layout. The shape stays what it was, so a field whose shape differs between the grids (a coarse fermion, say) needs a LayoutShapeScope instead. LayoutScope alone is useful for code that depends on the layout but not on the shape, such as Layout::latticeCoordinate, the Layout:: query functions, or seeding a layout's random number generator:

LatticeFermion mask(const LatticeFermion& in, int mu)
{
LayoutScope scope(in.layout());
LatticeReal x = Layout::latticeCoordinate(mu);   // on in's layout
return in * x;
}

docs.title: ShapeScope
docs.text:
explicit ShapeScope(const Shape& shape);
void close();

Pushes shape onto the shape stack and pops it at the end. The layout is not changed. close() works as for LayoutScope.

{
ShapeScope s(Shape(2, 7));
LatticeFermion psi;         // Ns=2, Nc=7, on the current layout
LatticeColorMatrix u;       // Nc=7 (a color matrix has no spin index)
LatticeReal r;              // no spin or color index
}

Each field takes from the shape only the extents its type has. See Shape.

docs.title: LayoutShapeScope
docs.text:
LayoutShapeScope(LatticeLayout layout, int ns, int nc);
template<class T> explicit LayoutShapeScope(const OLattice<T>& field);
void close();

Sets the layout and the shape together, the common case on a coarse grid. The first form takes them as arguments; the second takes field.layout() and field.shape(), so new fields match an existing one:

LatticeFermion make_like(const LatticeFermion& x)
{
LayoutShapeScope scope(x);
LatticeFermion y = zero;    // same layout and shape as x
return y;
}

close() restores both.

Take the scope from a field with spin and color

LayoutShapeScope(field) makes field.shape() current as it is. For a field without a spin index, such as a LatticeColorMatrix, that shape has Ns = 1, and a LatticeFermion created inside the scope then gets Ns = 1 as well. Use a fermion or propagator as the model, or pass the extents explicitly with LayoutShapeScope(field.layout(), ns, nc).

docs.title: JitDataFormatScope
docs.text:
explicit JitDataFormatScope(JitDataFormat format);

Sets the default data format for new fields and restores the previous one at the end. It has no close(); end it by ending the block.

JitDataFormat half(JitDataOrder::SiteFast, JitStorage::Half);
{
JitDataFormatScope scope(half);
LatticeColorMatrix u_half;     // stored in half precision
LatticeInteger     n;          // integer fields are always stored natively
}

It does not change the layout or the shape, and it applies on every layout. Integer and boolean fields always use native storage. See Data format.

docs.title: The typical multigrid pattern
docs.text:
A coarse-grid operation usually needs coarse fields and fine fields at the same time. Open a scope to declare the coarse fields, close it, and do the work with the fine grid current:

LatticeColorVector restrict_to_coarse(const LatticeFermion& psi,
const multi1d<LatticeFermion>& vecs,
const multi1d<int>& blocking)
{
const int nvec = vecs.size();

LayoutShapeScope coarse_grid(Layout::current().coarsen(blocking), 1, nvec);
LatticeColorVector psi_c;        // coarse, Nc=nvec
coarse_grid.close();             // the fine grid is current again

for (int i = 0; i < nvec; ++i)
{
LatticeComplex a = blockSum(localInnerProduct(vecs[i], psi), blocking);
pokeColor(psi_c, a, i);      // a and psi_c are on the coarse layout
}
return psi_c;
}

The coarse fields stay on the coarse layout after close(), so they can be used next to fine fields: blockSum takes a fine expression and returns a coarse field, and a mixed-layout expression such as fine = fine * coarse combines the two.

The opposite case, a fine temporary inside code that runs on the coarse grid, does not need a scope: construct it with OLattice(layout, shape).

docs.title: Nesting
docs.text:
Scopes can be nested to any depth, and the same layout can be opened again inside itself. At the end of each block the settings of the enclosing block are back.

Close scopes in reverse order

The layout and shape stacks are plain stacks: close() pops the top entry, whichever scope pushed it. If an outer scope is closed while an inner one is still open, the outer close() pops the inner layout and the outer one stays current:

LayoutScope a(coarse);
LayoutScope b(coarser);
a.close();                 // pops coarser: coarse is still current

Scopes that end with their blocks are always closed in the right order. Call close() only on the innermost open scope, and don't mix scopes with hand-written Layout::push/pop or Shape::push/pop that cross a scope boundary.

docs.title: Shape (Ns, Nc)
docs.text:
In QDP++ the number of spin components Ns and color components Nc are compile-time constants and template arguments of the primitive types (PSpinVector<T,Ns>, PColorMatrix<T,Nc>). In qdp-jit the primitive types have no extent argument (PSpinVector<T>, PColorMatrix<T>), and the extents are a run-time property of each field, its Shape. Fields of the same C++ type can therefore have different extents: a LatticeFermion with Ns = 4, Nc = 3 on the fine grid and one with Ns = 2, Nc = 24 on a coarse grid.

The constants Ns and Nc still exist. They are the values qdp-jit was configured with, and they make up the initial current shape: at start-up Shape::current() is Shape(Ns, Nc). Code that never changes the shape behaves as in QDP++.

docs.title: The Shape class
docs.text:
Shape s(2, 24);          // Ns = 2, Nc = 24
s.ns();                  // 2
s.nc();                  // 24
std::cout << s;          // Shape(ns=2, nc=24)

A field's shape is f.shape(), for lattice fields (OLattice) and for scalars (OScalar) alike.

docs.title: Which types use which extent
docs.text:
A field uses only the extents its type has. The other extent is stored as 1. Inside ShapeScope s(Shape(2, 5)), default-constructed fields get:

Type Shape LatticeReal, LatticeComplex, Complex (1, 1) LatticeColorVector, LatticeColorMatrix, ColorMatrix (1, 5) LatticeSpinVector, LatticeSpinMatrix (2, 1) LatticeFermion, LatticePropagator, Fermion (2, 5)

Some named types fix one extent and take the other from the current shape:

Type Ns Nc Inside ShapeScope(Shape(2, 5)) LatticeDiracFermion, LatticeDiracPropagator 4 current (4, 5) LatticeHalfFermion current Ns / 2 current (1, 5) LatticeStaggeredFermion 1 current (1, 5) LatticeFermionF3, LatticeFermionD3 current 3 (2, 3) LatticeColorMatrixF3, LatticeColorMatrixD3 (none) 3 (1, 3) LatticeDiracFermionF3, LatticeDiracFermionD3 4 3 (4, 3)

The table is for default construction. When one of these types is made from a plain field, for example LatticeDiracFermion d(f), it keeps f's extents on the axes it does not fix, and f must have the fixed extent (Ns = 4 here); otherwise the program aborts with OLattice: Incompatible tensor dimensions.

docs.title: The current shape
docs.text:
The shape of a default-constructed field comes from the top of the shape stack, Shape::current(). Change it with a ShapeScope or, together with the layout, with a LayoutShapeScope:

{
ShapeScope s(Shape(2, 24));
LatticeFermion psi;          // (2, 24)
LatticeColorMatrix u;        // (1, 24)
}
LatticeFermion chi;            // (Ns, Nc) again

Shape::push and Shape::pop change the stack directly; prefer the scopes, which pop automatically. Shape::pop or Shape::current on an empty stack aborts with Shape::pop: Shape stack is empty or Shape::current: Shape stack is empty.

A field keeps its shape for its whole life. Changing the current shape does not change existing fields.

docs.title: Creating a field with a given shape
docs.text:
Instead of changing the current shape, pass the shape to the constructor:

LatticeFermion psi(Shape(2, 24));          // on the current layout
LatticeFermion chi(Shape(2, 24), zero);    // and set to zero
LatticeFermion eta(coarse, Shape(2, 24));  // on a given layout, see Layouts
Fermion        f(Shape(2, 24));            // scalars too

Extents the type lacks are dropped: LatticeColorMatrix u(Shape(4, 3)) has shape (1, 3). A field made by a copy or from an expression takes the shape of the source; an index the source's type does not have takes its extent from the current shape, so LatticeColorMatrix m = r + r with r a LatticeReal has Nc from Shape::current(). See also Construction and copying.

docs.title: How expressions combine shapes
docs.text:
The shape of an expression is worked out from its leaves, operation by operation:

  1. The shapes of the operands are merged extent by extent. An operand whose type has no spin index (or no color index) takes no part in that extent, so a LatticeComplex times a LatticeFermion (2, 5) gives (2, 5). Operands that have the index must agree on its extent, even when it is 1.
  2. A few operations change an extent (see below).
  3. Extents the result type lacks are dropped.
Expression (with psi, prop of shape (2, 5)) Result shape u * psi, u a LatticeColorMatrix (1, 5) (2, 5) c * psi, c a LatticeComplex (2, 5) shift(psi, FORWARD, mu) + psi (2, 5) traceSpin(prop), traceSpin(outerProduct(psi, psi)) (1, 5) traceColor(prop) (2, 1) trace(prop), localInnerProduct(psi, psi) (1, 1) peekSpin(psi, s) (1, 5) peekColor(peekSpin(psi, s), c) (1, 1) sum(psi) a FermionD of shape (2, 5) innerProduct(psi, psi), norm2(psi) a scalar, (1, 1)

Operations that change an extent:

Operation Requires Result spinProjectDir* Ns = 4 Ns = 2 spinReconstructDir* Ns = 2 Ns = 4 Gamma(n) * x Ns = 4 Ns = 4

Operands that have an index but disagree on its extent cannot be combined. The program aborts when the expression is evaluated:

Cause Message u * psi with u (1, 3), psi (2, 5) Cannot combine incompatible extents 3 and 5 cv1 + cv5, color vectors with Nc = 1 and Nc = 5 Cannot combine incompatible extents 1 and 5 Gamma(n) * psi with Ns = 2 Cannot combine incompatible extents 4 and 2 spinProjectDir0Minus(psi) with Ns = 2 Spin projection requires Ns=4; got Ns=2 spinReconstructDir0Minus(h) with Ns ≠ 2 Spin reconstruction requires Ns=2; got Ns=…

docs.title: Assignment
docs.text:
Assigning to a lattice field keeps the field's shape. The right-hand side must have the same extents, except for an index its type does not have: a number or a LatticeReal can be assigned to a color matrix of any Nc (u = 1.0 sets every color matrix to the unit matrix). Otherwise the program aborts, also for += and the other compound assignments:

LatticeFermion psi;                 // (4, 3)
LatticeFermion chi(Shape(2, 5));
psi = chi;
// OLattice: Incompatible tensor dimensions: lhs=(Nc=3,Ns=4), rhs=(Nc=5,Ns=2)

Scalars (OScalar) behave differently: when the right-hand side's shape does not fit, the scalar takes the new shape.

Fermion x;                          // (4, 3)
Fermion c(Shape(2, 12));
x = c;                              // x is now (2, 12)

This lets a scalar hold the result of sum or peekSite on any grid without knowing the shape in advance.

docs.title: Timing
docs.text: qdp-jit runs each expression as a kernel on the GPU. Kernel launches are asynchronous: chi = u * psi returns as soon as the kernel is queued, before it has run. A host timer started and stopped around a few lines of code therefore measures how long it took to queue the kernels, not how long they ran, and the work that was queued shows up in whatever is timed next.

docs.title: StopWatch
docs.text:
StopWatch is the QDP++ timer:

StopWatch sw;
sw.reset();
sw.start();
for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i)
chi = u * psi;
sw.stop();
QDPIO::cout << "time: " << sw.getTimeInSeconds() << " s" << std::endl;

When the program runs with the command-line option

-timing-run

start() and stop() first wait until the GPU has finished all work queued so far. The time between them is then the time the GPU took for the work queued in between. Without -timing-run, start() and stop() do not wait, and the times are wrong.

On one GPU, 2000 launches of chi = u * psi on a 16^4 lattice:

Measured without -timing-run 11 ms, the time to queue 2000 kernels; the kernels run later with -timing-run 23 ms, the time the kernels took

The program prints whether -timing-run is on at start-up, in the line Accurate timing : 1.

Waiting for the GPU costs time, and it stops the host from queueing work ahead. Use -timing-run for timing runs, not for production runs.

StopWatch(false) makes a stopwatch that never waits, even with -timing-run. Use it to measure host time only, for example the time spent queueing kernels.

Any operation that brings a result back to the host waits for the GPU too: norm2, sum, innerProduct, peekSite and the other reductions return a value on the host, so they include all work queued before them. A timed block that ends with a reduction is therefore timed correctly even without -timing-run, but it then includes the reduction.

docs.title: The first call compiles the kernel
docs.text:
The first time an expression is evaluated, qdp-jit generates and compiles a kernel for it, which takes several milliseconds. Later evaluations reuse the kernel:

Evaluation Time first chi = u * psi 11 ms (compilation) second chi = u * psi 0.03 ms

A kernel is reused for the same expression on other fields of the same types, on another subset and on another layout. A new kernel is compiled for a new expression, and also for the same expression on fields with a different shape or data format, or when the destination also appears on the right-hand side (chi = u * chi after chi = u * psi).

To time the work and not the compilation, run the code once before timing it:

chi = u * psi;                 // warm-up: compiles the kernel

StopWatch sw;
sw.start();
for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i)
chi = u * psi;
sw.stop();

At the end of the run, QDP_finalize prints how many kernels were compiled and how long the compilation took in total:

Code generator
  functions jit-compiled (GPU)             27
  total time for IR builder:               0.008144 s
  total time for libm IR linking:          0.003707 s
  total time for IR passes:                0.002814 s
  total time for code generation:          0.137968 s
  total time for dynamic loading:          0.002633 s

A number of compiled kernels that grows with the length of the run means that new kernels keep being made, for example for fields with ever new shapes.

docs.title: Kernel statistics
docs.text:
The command-line option

-stats

times every kernel launch on the GPU. At the end of the run, QDP_finalize prints a table of all kernels, sorted by their total time:

#   calls  stack  regs  cmem  sum(ms)     mean      stddev    name
1   8005   0      64    0     102.313667  0.012781  0.000528  eval5
8   3      0      44    0     0.078720    0.026240  0.003231  reduce_expr0
...
Column Meaning calls number of launches stack local memory per thread (stack and register spills), in bytes regs registers per thread cmem constant memory, in bytes sum(ms), mean, stddev total, mean and standard deviation of the kernel's run time, in milliseconds name the kernel's name

On AMD GPUs, the columns stack, regs and cmem are replaced by the register and memory counts of that platform.

The same table is written to the file qdp_jit_stats.txt in the working directory, with two extra columns for register spills, which are filled in only on some platforms. After the table, the file lists each kernel's name with the C++ types of the expression it was generated for, which tells which kernel belongs to which line of code.

-stats waits for each kernel to finish before the next one is launched, so the program runs slower: the 2000 launches above take 41 ms instead of 23 ms. Use it to find which kernels take the time, and StopWatch with -timing-run to measure the time of a piece of code. The statistics are collected on the primary rank only.
